profile.name: Clarence Neil Meneses
profile.headline: Full-Stack Web Developer \ Data Analyst
profile.about:
I'm a full-stack developer and a BS Information Technology graduate of Batangas State University, major in Business Analytics (Class of 2026).

I build the systems small businesses run on. Right now that's Malaya Villas, a private rental business with ten villas: I built its booking site and staff back office on React, TypeScript, and Supabase, and on October 1 it replaced the owner's spreadsheets for every villa, with Xendit checkout and Airbnb calendar sync so nothing double-books.

I'm also the founding developer of PapaFix, a funded home-services marketplace under NAM Builders Supply Corp. They retained me after my internship, where I built the company's first sales platform, now handling ₱1M+ in monthly sales. I built PapaFix's web platform, and in November I redesigned both of its mobile apps, customer and technician, on one shared design kit. For the same company I'm now building a KPI board that scores its three businesses against one scorecard.

I design the interfaces I build, and I make product walkthrough films in code with Remotion, for my own projects and on commission. On the side I also build Shopify stores: custom Liquid product pages and a catalog pipeline for a German beauty brand.

I work across React, TypeScript, React Native, PostgreSQL, PHP, Shopify, and REST APIs, and I ship through reviewed pull requests with a test checklist for every change. Google-certified in Analytics and Ads Measurement.

projects.title: Malaya OBS — Villa Operations & Business System
projects.description: The booking site and staff back office a ten-villa rental business runs on: bookings, Xendit payments, Airbnb calendar sync, finance and owner P&L. It replaced the owner's spreadsheets on October 1.
projects.tech: React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Start, TanStack Router, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Row Level Security, Xendit, Airbnb iCal, Claude API, Recharts, Vercel

blocks.text: Malaya Villas rents out ten private villas, and until this year the business ran on spreadsheets and Messenger threads. In August 2026 I took on Malaya OBS as its developer. What I was handed was a click-through prototype: no database, no login, no public site, and every number invented in the browser. The job was to turn it into the system the company actually runs on.
What I built

A booking website for guests and a back office for staff, on one Supabase Postgres database with row-level security per role. A guest picks dates and pays on the public site; the stay blocks the calendar, the payment lands in Finance, and staff see the next step on the booking page. Around that loop sit the calendar and pricing, an inbox, maintenance, team roles, and the owner's reports.
Going live

On October 1 the system replaced the owner's spreadsheets as the record for all ten villas. Before the switch I imported each villa's booking and cash-flow workbook and reconciled it line by line, and every month since is crosschecked against the sheets, ending in a to-do list for the staff. Guests pay through Xendit checkout, and nine villa calendars sync with Airbnb, so nothing gets double-booked.
A database that refuses to be wrong

Business rules live in constraints, not just TypeScript. Money is numeric, stay dates are calendar dates so Manila bookings never drift a day on a UTC server, and a GiST exclusion constraint makes a double booking physically impossible. A trigger on every table writes an audit log, so every change shows up as a plain sentence: who did what to which booking.
Security in the database, not the sidebar

Staff, owners and guests share the same tables. The sidebar hides tabs and screens refuse actions, but only Postgres policies are the real boundary: a caretaker cannot read the P&L even by calling the API directly. When the owner asked for custom roles, roles became data, so policies check has_permission() instead of naming a role, and staff can be scoped to only the villas they are assigned.
Finance built to the owner's own workbooks

The owner's spreadsheets outranked the spec for Finance, so the module was built to match them cell by cell: per-villa monthly P&L, owner earnings and cash position, with breakdowns that drill down to each receipt. The importers were ported from Python to TypeScript line for line, with a verifier that had to print IDENTICAL before either changed. Payments and expenses only count once a person has verified them.
Designed for the people using it

Eighteen staff use it every day. When some of them missed that an action was a button at all, I gave the interface a small, strict vocabulary: brown for the main step, green to confirm, red to remove, white for everything safe, every clickable word underlined, and a confirmation that names the guest, the amount and the booking code before any one-click approval. Depth comes from shades instead of lines, and related controls sit together in rounded pills. This portfolio follows the same rules, and so do the PapaFix mobile apps I redesigned afterwards.
Payments and AI, kept honest

Online payments go through Xendit, and the webhook records the payment and confirms the booking in one transaction. Maya, the built-in assistant, is a real Claude call over the figures already on screen. It is never allowed to query the database or calculate a number itself, so it can never disagree with the Finance tab.
Since the switch-over

The system has kept growing with the business. The owner now gets a report by email every night. Receipts are filed in folders that download as one archive. Xendit's fees are reconciled against the gateway's own records. The P&L was rebuilt around one date rule, with a break-even per villa and a forecast. Investors sign in to see only their own branch, and affiliates earn a share of the bookings they bring.
How I work

Every change ships through a pull request the owner reviews, more than 150 so far, each with a test checklist that says who checks what, and I recorded a training video for the staff. Type-checking and tests now run on every pull request before it can merge. This is the project where I learned to own a system a business depends on: reading a spec closely enough to find its contradictions, asking the questions only the owner can answer, and refusing to invent a number. It is ongoing.

projects.title: PapaFix Mobile: Customer & Technician Apps
projects.description: A full UI/UX redesign of both Android apps on one shared design kit: 40+ screens, a guided booking flow and a mascot with 14 poses, shipped over the air with no new store build.
projects.tech: React Native, Expo, Expo Router, TypeScript, Supabase, EAS Update

blocks.text: PapaFix has two Android apps on Google Play: one where customers book an aircon, plumbing or electrical technician, and one where technicians take and finish those jobs. Both worked, but they had grown one screen at a time. An audit found about 150 hand-bordered cards, no shared button, and type as small as 9 points. In November 2026 I redesigned both apps without changing how anything works.

blocks.caption: The customer app after the redesign, in the Google Play listing art I designed for it.

blocks.text: One kit, two apps

The two apps live in one monorepo and share a package, so the redesign started there: colour and spacing tokens, a card, one button with a few tones, a text field, status pills, tab pills, list cards and stat tiles. Every screen in both apps was then rebuilt from those pieces. The customer app is blue and the technician app is orange, and that accent is the only thing that differs between them.
The same language as Malaya

The look follows the design language I built for Malaya Villas' back office: depth from shades instead of drawn lines, related controls grouped in rounded pills, the open tab as a soft fill, and one typeface at light weights under spaced small-caps labels. The bottom navigation is a floating pill with a separate round + button that opens the app's main actions.
Booking, one decision at a time

Booking a technician became a four-step flow with a progress bar and a card for each decision. The price stays pinned to the bottom of the screen the whole way through, so a customer sees what they will pay before they commit. Aircon, plumbing and electrical get the same treatment, each with its own colour and icon.

blocks.caption: The + menu and Help & Support.
The technician app: home, incoming jobs, and the schedule where a technician sets their hours.

blocks.text: Papa, the mascot

The apps' mascot, Papa, used to appear only on the launch screen. I produced a set of 14 poses in one consistent style, generated from the original art and cleaned up by hand, and gave him a job. He greets you on the home screen, searches while a technician is being matched, shrugs at an empty list, and owns up when something fails to load. Every full-screen loading spinner in both apps became Papa.

blocks.caption: Papa's 14 poses, each tied to a moment in the app.

blocks.text: Shipped without a store release

The redesign changed 91 files, and none of it needed a new build. I kept every change inside JavaScript and compared each branch's native fingerprint with the released apps', so the mobile lead could publish it over the air and users got the new look the next time they opened the app. The one native change, a cleaner launch screen, went into its own pull request to wait for the next store build.
How I worked

It is another developer's codebase, so everything went through pull requests he reviewed: three merged within two days. To test, I set up an Android emulator and local builds of both apps. Along the way I found and fixed a bug older than the redesign, where customers who skipped entering a name were bounced away from every Book button.

projects.title: PapaFix — Home-Services Marketplace Platform
projects.description: The web platform a funded home-repair marketplace runs on: 15 modules for bookings, technician onboarding, payment settlement, pricing and live dispatch, backed by a 292-case test suite.
projects.tech: React 19, Vite, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Edge Functions, RLS, Leaflet, Recharts

blocks.text: PapaFix is an on-demand home-repair marketplace for the Philippines, a funded venture under NAM Builders Supply Corp: customers book electricians, plumbers, and aircon technicians from one mobile app, while technicians accept and complete those jobs from another — both now on Google Play. The two apps write to a single Supabase Postgres database, but the business had no way to actually oversee the operation — which jobs were stalling, which payments hadn't cleared, where technicians were in the field, or whether a record had been quietly altered. As founding developer I built the web platform that sits over all of it: the control room for the entire business.
What I built

I designed and developed a dark-mode admin panel in React and Supabase that reads, oversees, and corrects everything the two mobile apps generate. The customer app, the technician app, and this panel all share one Postgres database — the apps own the operational writes, and the panel is the layer that gives the business visibility and control over them. It is locked to admin accounts only, enforced not just in the UI but by Postgres row-level security, so it holds full oversight without ever shipping a service key to the browser.
Day-to-day operations

blocks.caption: The Profiles tab managing customers, technicians, and admins, with role filters and server-side user creation.

blocks.text: The management tabs cover the operational core. I built full create-read-update-delete for user profiles — searchable and role-filtered across customers, technicians, and admins, with base location, service categories and service radius for technicians — and routed account creation and email changes through a secure server-side Edge Function so the service key never touches the browser. Bookings get the same treatment with status, category, payment, and date filters plus a full detail view down to the inspection checklist and on-site QR token. Alongside these sit saved customer locations with inline map previews, a technician availability scheduler with per-slot toggles, and a support-ticket queue with status and priority.
Seeing the field in real time

Because technicians work in the field, the panel tracks them in real time. The Live Map renders every technician on an interactive Leaflet map — green when online, grey when offline — alongside the blue pins of active customer job sites, and it auto-refreshes on its own. A companion Tech Locations view lists each technician's last-known coordinates and how long ago they reported in, for when I need the data as a table rather than a map.

blocks.caption: The Live Map tracking technicians (online and offline) and customer job sites in real time across Batangas.

blocks.text: Pricing and getting paid

A marketplace is only as trustworthy as its prices, so the panel owns them outright. I built a pricing surface where an admin sets the aircon price grid and per-category base prices, then layers on the add-on admin fee, VAT, and distance-banded travel-fee tiers — the same numbers the customer app quotes upfront, edited in one place instead of hard-coded in an app release. Payment is the other half: a verification queue moves jobs through awaiting, paid, and unpaid, with cash-proof photos reviewed and rejected with a reason, and settlement handled by a dedicated Edge Function rather than a client-side write. A separate tab manages the GCash, Maya, and bank QR codes customers actually pay against.
Analytics and insight

The Overview dashboard is the at-a-glance health check: headline KPIs against the previous period, a bookings-and-revenue trend, demand patterns by hour and weekday, a top-technicians leaderboard, a per-city revenue split with an adjustable manager-share percentage, and a needs-attention queue that surfaces stale jobs, unpaid completed work, and low ratings. The Analytics tab goes deeper, with drill-downs by category, status, and payment, and a technician ranking where clicking one bar cross-filters every chart on the page. Both started out pulling thousands of raw booking rows into the browser to crunch client-side, which doesn't scale — so I moved all of that aggregation into PostgreSQL functions that return pre-summarised JSON, backed by targeted indexes and server-side pagination so the panel stays responsive into the hundreds of thousands of rows.

blocks.caption: The Analytics tab with a technician selected — one click cross-filters every chart on the page.

blocks.text: Oversight and integrity

Oversight only means something if the records can be trusted. The audit trail records every booking and payment event the moment a row changes — created, status moved, technician reassigned, payment captured, fee adjusted — written by Postgres triggers through a SECURITY DEFINER function under row-level security with no update or delete policy, so even an admin can't forge or erase one. I deliberately scoped it to the facts that change a record rather than taps, locations, or message contents: a complete paper trail without surveilling users. A separate activity log captures what admins themselves do inside the panel, keeping the two concerns cleanly apart.

blocks.caption: The append-only audit trail, with every booking and payment event recorded server-side by database triggers.

blocks.text: Admin itself is tiered rather than all-or-nothing: a roles-and-access screen, reachable only by a super admin, decides which admins can touch pricing, payments, or accounts. Beside it sits a user-reports queue where misconduct reports filed in either direction — customer against technician, or technician against customer — are triaged, so the same trail that protects the records also protects the people using them.
Conclusion

PapaFix is the project where I owned an entire operational surface end to end — from the React interface down to the Postgres triggers, RPCs, row-level security policies, and the Edge Functions that keep privileged work off the client. The throughline was building for scale and trust: aggregate on the server so it holds up as the data grows, and push integrity into the database where it can't be bypassed. It is the clearest example of how I think about full-stack work — that the hard guarantees belong close to the data, and the browser is just an untrusted client looking in.

projects.title: Product Walkthrough Films: Motion Graphics
projects.description: Motion-graphics films that walk through an app one action at a time. Built in code with Remotion, for my own projects and on commission.

blocks.text: I make product films the way I make products: in code. Each one is a React project rendered with Remotion, so a screen in the film is a real component, a wrong number is fixed by changing a line, and a new cut is a re-render instead of a re-edit.
FixLink: app walkthrough (commission)

blocks.caption: FixLink app walkthrough, 2:30. Every name, address and price in it is invented.

blocks.text: FixLink is a home-services app concept from a student's research, and the brief was a film that explains it from sign-up to review. I followed the client's own flow chart: nine steps, each shown on one phone, with the step's name on the left and a callout on the right. The app's screens are rebuilt as clean cards and made to work. A fingertip taps, fields fill in, a quote adds up, and the camera leans in on each tap. The soundtrack is written in code too, timed to the cuts, with a sound for every tap.
Malaya Villas: guest features

blocks.caption: Malaya Villas guest features, one minute.

blocks.text: Made for the villa business whose booking system I build. It shows the guest's side, from searching dates to signing the waiver, one feature per beat, in the brand's own type and colours.
PapaFix: product reel

blocks.caption: PapaFix product reel, 63 seconds. Also cut in 9:16 for social.

blocks.text: A reel for the home-services app: booking, matching, live tracking, the QR check at the door, and payment. It comes in a wide cut and a vertical cut that share every frame and one soundtrack.
Why code

A film built this way stays editable for as long as the product does. When a screen changes, I change the component and render again. I made a seven-minute training video for Malaya's staff the same way, from real screens with guest names replaced, so the people using the system could learn it without having to explore on their own.
Music in the FixLink film uses the Salamander Grand Piano by Alexander Holm (CC BY 3.0), with instruments from Versilian Studios, FreePats and Karoryfer Samples.

projects.title: Mainframe: KPI Board for Three Businesses
projects.description: A board that scores a company's three businesses against one weighted KPI scorecard, with every score traceable to the figures behind it.
projects.tech: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Row Level Security, Recharts

blocks.text: NAM's CEO runs three businesses and grades them on one scorecard: nine categories, from sales and finance to quality and governance, each with a weight, adding up to 100. He asked for a board that shows where each business stands without anyone compiling a spreadsheet. It is phase one of a larger internal system, started in November 2026.
What it shows

One screen answers the first question: a group score, a heatmap of businesses against categories, and a list of what is costing the most points, ranked. Every tile opens the list behind it, every score opens a breakdown of where it came from, and a twelve-month trend sits against the target.
Scoring that can be explained

A score nobody can explain gets ignored, so the rules are plain. Attainment is capped at 100 percent, so one great month cannot hide a weak category. A figure nobody reported shows as a gap instead of counting as a zero. A "How it works" page walks through the arithmetic using the board's own live numbers.
Real figures, not typed ones

For the supply business, sales, margin and collections are read straight from the sales platform I built for the company earlier, so the board and the system of record cannot disagree. For figures that only exist on paper, staff enter two counts, such as 19 out of 20, and the board works out the percentage.
Private by default

The board shows what clients owe, so nothing on it is public and there are no screenshots here. Editors sign in. The CEO opens a private view link that reads the board through a single database function, while the tables themselves stay closed.
It is live. The supply business is loaded from January 2026 onward, and the other two are waiting on their first figures.

projects.title: NAM Builders Supply Corp — Sales & Inventory Platform
projects.description: The company's first sales system — quotations, inventory, and finance in one place, now running ₱1M+ in monthly operations.
projects.tech: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Supabase, PostgreSQL, TanStack Query, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Vitest, PHP, MySQL

blocks.text: NAM Builders Supply Corp was running a building-supply business on spreadsheets. Quotations were typed by hand, sales lived in one workbook and inventory in another, and putting a single report in front of management meant a week of chasing files across departments. I joined as an IT intern for a 500-hour internship and built the company its first real system.
What I built

I replaced the spreadsheet workflow with one platform covering quotations, sales entry, the sales ledger, products and stock, finance, logistics, and bulk imports. It is now used daily by staff to run over ₱1M in monthly sales operations. The goal was never to digitise the spreadsheets — it was to make the numbers agree with each other for the first time.

blocks.caption: The executive dashboard — sales performance and key metrics in one view, replacing a week of manual compilation.

blocks.text: Quotation to sale

The core workflow moves a quotation through drafting and approval into a confirmed sale, deducting stock as it goes. Quotations print in the company's existing formal document format, so staff did not have to change how they present to clients, and a quote can be converted partially when a client only takes some of the line items. Deliveries carry their own DR numbers through logistics, and finance tracks receivables against payment status.

blocks.caption: Inventory management — centralized supplier pricing with bulk CSV import.

blocks.text: Numbers that reconcile

On top of the operational data I built a reporting layer: an executive view with cross-filtering drilldowns by company, category, and account manager. The hard part was trust, not charts. I wrote the pricing and margin logic — income, markup and margin solvers, withholding tax, and the formal-document arithmetic — as a unit-tested calculation engine, so that what the dashboard shows reconciles with what finance calculates by hand.
Re-architecting on Postgres

The system shipped first in PHP and MySQL. I later re-architected it as a React and TypeScript single-page app on Supabase, which meant moving years of live production data without losing any of it. I wrote the migration myself: a converter that reads the legacy MySQL dump, scrubs currency-formatted values back into numerics, normalises malformed and zero dates, and corrects timezone handling that would otherwise have shifted historical records by a day. A Legacy Restore screen inside the app lets that import be re-run and checked rather than trusted blindly.
Who can see what

Several departments touch the same record, so access is a first-class feature rather than a checkbox. Roles and per-privilege gates are defined in the database and enforced by row-level security, account managers are assigned to the companies they handle, sessions are limited to one active login per account, and an activity log records who changed what. The frontend only ever holds the publishable key.

I finished the internship with a full handover — per-module technical documentation plus training, so staff could run their own reporting without me. The system stayed in daily use after I left, which is the part I judge it by.

projects.title: Portfolio Revamped: Portfolio & CMS
projects.description: A self-hosted portfolio with a built-in admin CMS, where every section is editable without redeploying.
projects.tech: Next.js 14, React, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Tailwind CSS, Vercel

blocks.text: I wanted a portfolio I could keep current without touching code or redeploying every time. So I rebuilt mine as a fully content-managed site: every section, from my profile and tech stack to projects, experience, certifications, and gallery, is editable from a private admin panel.
What I built

blocks.caption: The admin CMS, where I edit and reorder every section of the live site.

blocks.text: I built it on Next.js 14 with the App Router and Tailwind CSS, backed by Supabase for Postgres, Auth, and image Storage. The admin lives at /admin behind Supabase Auth, and I deliberately kept all secret keys out of the app. Every write is gated by row-level security, so the public site only ever uses the publishable key.
Everything is editable

There are no hard-coded sections. I manage projects, work history, skills, certifications, social links, and gallery photos directly in the CMS, with drag-and-drop reordering. Slugs are generated automatically, drafts stay hidden until I publish, and changes appear on the live site within seconds.
The challenge: free-tier cold starts

Supabase pauses free projects after about a week of inactivity, which would leave a portfolio loading slowly or blank. I solved this in three layers: a daily keep-alive cron that pings a lightweight endpoint so the project never registers as idle, ISR caching so visitors always get an instant cached page, and a bundled fallback snapshot that renders the site from local content if the database is ever truly unreachable.
SEO that maintains itself

Per-page titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and Open Graph and Twitter tags are generated from the same CMS content. A sitemap that includes every published case study and a robots.txt are produced automatically, so my SEO stays correct as I add new work, with no manual upkeep.

The result is the site you are viewing right now. I can publish a new project or swap an image in seconds, with no deploy and no downtime. It is the foundation I use to keep my entire portfolio current.

projects.title: Lexus Industrial — Catalog Website & CMS
projects.description: A production catalog site with a role-secured admin dashboard, so staff manage the product range themselves.
projects.tech: React, TypeScript, Vite, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Tailwind CSS, GSAP

blocks.text: A product catalog is the worst possible thing to hard-code. The range changes, prices move, photos get replaced — and if every one of those edits needs a developer and a deploy, the site is out of date within weeks and the business stops trusting it. So the brief was less "build a website" than "build something the staff can own".
What I built

I built the public site and its admin dashboard as one React and TypeScript application on Supabase. Visitors get a catalog with product listings and detail pages, services, company information, and an enquiry form. Staff sign in to an admin area covering products with image upload, categories, the enquiries that come in through the site, editable page content, user accounts, and settings — no developer in the loop, no redeploy.
Three tiers of access

Not everyone who edits the site should be able to create logins for it, so I modelled access as three roles rather than a single admin flag: admin, editor, and viewer. The distinction is enforced by row-level security in Postgres, not by hiding buttons — an editor who forged a request would still be refused by the database. Creating and deleting login accounts genuinely needs a privileged key, so I moved that into a Supabase Edge Function that checks the caller is an admin before it acts, which keeps the service key on the server where it belongs.
Finding things

An industrial catalog is only useful if you can find the one part you came for. I used Postgres full-text search rather than filtering in the browser, so the work happens where the data is and search keeps up as the catalog grows. Product images live in their own storage bucket with its own policies, and every query in the app goes through a single typed API layer, so the shape of the data is checked at compile time instead of discovered in production.

What I like about this one is how boring it became to maintain. The catalog stays current because the people who actually know the products are the ones editing it, and the security model means handing someone a login is a low-stakes decision rather than a risk.

projects.title: NAM Builders Supply Corp — Official Website
projects.description: A public company site backed by a custom CMS, so staff can keep it current without a developer.
projects.tech: PHP, MySQL, JavaScript, Bootstrap, HTML5, CSS3

blocks.text: With the internal system in place, NAM still had no public presence — clients found them by word of mouth or by walking in. They needed a site that showed their materials and services, and more importantly one they could keep current themselves. A static page would have been out of date within a month.

blocks.caption: The public site — product categories, services, and company information.

blocks.text: A CMS, not a static site

So I built the site on a custom content management system in PHP and MySQL rather than hard-coding the pages. The front end is a responsive Bootstrap layout — hero, company profile, a services gallery, and a continuously scrolling client carousel — but every one of those sections reads from the database. Staff sign in to a secure admin dashboard and manage services, clients, business statistics, and incoming enquiries directly. Nobody needs to touch code, and nobody needs to call me to change a price list.

blocks.caption: The admin dashboard where staff manage site content and client messages.

blocks.text: Building the admin side was the real work — session-guarded login, input validation on every write, image upload and replacement for services and client logos, and an editing flow simple enough that non-technical staff would actually use it rather than reverting to phone calls. Contact-form submissions land in the same dashboard, so an enquiry is a record to work through rather than an email someone might miss.

blocks.caption: Content updates writing straight to the database and appearing live on the site.

blocks.text: The site is deployed as the company's primary online presence, and staff update it themselves. Paired with the internal sales platform, it means both sides of the business — what clients see and what the company runs on — are systems the company owns rather than documents they maintain by hand.

projects.title: PDAO Helps: PWD Services & Data Management System
projects.description: A constituent-services portal for a city PWD affairs office — ID applications, appointments, and demographic mapping across 30 barangays.
projects.tech: PHP, MySQL, JavaScript, Leaflet.js, Chart.js, GIS Mapping, Web Accessibility

blocks.text: The Persons with Disability Affairs Office of Sto. Tomas ran on paper. Every ID application, renewal, and appointment for the city's roughly 4,000 registered PWDs moved through physical forms and in-person visits, so constituents travelled to the office just to check a status and staff had no way to see the data as a whole. I built this portal as my capstone project, under a memorandum of agreement with the city government.

blocks.caption: The public-facing portal featuring a custom-built accessibility widget for inclusive navigation.

blocks.text: A core requirement was ensuring the platform was truly usable by its target audience. I engineered a dedicated Accessibility Widget that allows users to toggle High Contrast Mode, Grayscale, and Dyslexia-Friendly fonts without relying on third-party overlays. This required writing extensive CSS overrides and JavaScript handlers to dynamically manipulate the DOM in real-time.

blocks.caption: The multi-step application form that handles personal data, document uploads, and scheduling.

blocks.text: The system features a comprehensive backend to handle PWD ID applications and appointment bookings. I implemented a secure file upload system for sensitive documents (like medical certificates) and a scheduling algorithm that prevents overbooking by checking daily slot limits against the database. Applicants receive a unique reference number to track their status online, reducing the need for physical follow-ups.

blocks.caption: The administrative command center providing real-time insights into application processing and daily schedules.

blocks.text: To assist local government in resource allocation, I built a GIS (Geographic Information System) module using Leaflet.js. This feature visualizes the distribution of PWDs across different barangays using interactive markers and choropleth layers. It allows officials to filter data by disability type or status, identifying specific areas that may require targeted medical missions or support programs.

blocks.caption: Interactive geospatial map helping administrators visualize PWD density across barangays.

blocks.text: The Analytics module transforms raw database records into actionable insights. Using Chart.js, I created dynamic visualizations for demographic data, including age distribution, gender, and employment status. The system also generates printable PDF reports, automating what used to be a tedious manual compilation process for monthly reporting.

I verified the system through structured testing and UAT with office staff before turnover. Throughout development and every demo, the database held synthetic records I generated to match the city's real per-barangay PWD counts — realistic enough to prove the reporting worked, without a single real constituent record ever leaving the office. It was handed over as a system the staff could run themselves.
